intro.title: We designed a flying fish from first principles, and built the machine that checks it
intro.standfirst: Three days, five systems, and a serious attempt at the thing biology has never had: a way to check a design before you build the animal.
body: Mathematics has a button. A mathematician writes a proof, hands it to a program called a proof assistant, and the program verifies every step — not *probably*, not *as far as a reviewer could tell*, but checked. Biology has never had that button. A biologist with a design has intuition, experience, and an experiment that takes a year.
We spent a hackathon building the button.

You describe an organism in plain English. Ours was *a zebrafish with wings that glides over the water*. The system turns that sentence into a specification in real units, then works downwards — organ systems, organs, tissues, cell types, signalling pathways, genes, the specific letters of DNA you would have to change, and how every one of those has to behave as the animal grows up. Nine layers, each tied to standard biological vocabulary, so a biologist can argue with any single step.

Then it checks the result. Against formal laws written in **Lean**, the same proof assistant mathematicians use, where we proved real theorems from population genetics — Kimura, Fisher, Maynard Smith — and wired them into a registry a design is tested against. Against real protein alignments, built with the standard tool from real genomes, comparing our predicted fish to flying fishes that actually exist. And against a physics simulator that works out whether the thing could get out of the water.

The answer on that last one was no, and we kept it on the front page. The simulator found our fish would reach 0.67 metres per second at launch and needs 8.64. We mention this not out of modesty but because it is the most useful thing the machine did all weekend: it told us something true about our own idea that we did not want to hear, in about four seconds, for no money. The alternative way to learn that fact involves a lab, a year, and a grant.

Everything else worked. The claim engine read Darwin, Thompson, Aristotle, Wolfram and Michael Levin across seven separate source corpora, and broke them into 1,763 single checkable statements. The whole system is callable by an AI agent through 58 tools, because if software is going to design biology then software has to be able to check it. The designs come out as files you can print — we printed them — and as genetic sequences you could in principle hand to a lab.

What follows is five short posts, one per piece, in plain English. If you want the structure and the commands, there is a technical skim. If you want everything, including every way we watched it break, there is a deep version. Both are one click away, and neither of them is this one.

nanopubs.title: Aristotle, at One Claim Per Second
nanopubs.standfirst: How five canonical books became 1,763 individually checkable statements — and what happened when we started checking them.
body: Books are arguments. Data is rows. The gap between those two things is where most of biology's accumulated knowledge quietly sits, unusable by any machine, and closing it was the first thing we built. We took five primary corpora apart sentence by sentence and turned them into single checkable claims: one statement, one source, a locator precise enough to find it again — a chapter for Darwin, D'Arcy Thompson and Wolfram, work/book/section for Aristotle, paper and section for Levin — and, for 1,735 of the claims, the verbatim passage it came from, so nobody has to trust our paraphrase. The 28 without one — 23 math-biology theorems and 5 plant-mechanics entries — carry a paper title and year instead, Fisher and Turing and Kimura having written the sentences we would otherwise have had to quote. By the end of the weekend there were 1,763 of them.

Aristotle's biology gave up 566 claims, Wolfram's *A New Kind of Science* 321, Michael Levin's papers 310, D'Arcy Thompson's *On Growth and Form* 291 and Darwin's *Origin* 247, with math-biology (23) and plant-mechanics (5) sets bringing the total to 1,763 claims from seven claim sources. There are eight claim-source projects in the repository, but the eighth extracts no claims of its own: it is a Cellpose segmentation pipeline that produces evidence for three Thompson claims. These are not summaries. They are the smallest units of the books that can be right or wrong on their own, which turns out to be the only size a computer can do anything useful with.

Then the triage question: which of these could actually be settled against data that exists in public? Each of the 1,735 quoted claims was assessed for dataset-resolvability by two independent frontier models from different providers — OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and xAI's Grok 4.7 — each asked separately whether the claim was resolvable and what dataset would do it, with a third assessor, a Qwen3-32B we hosted ourselves on an NVIDIA L40S, taking a second pass over all 566 Aristotle claims: 4,036 assessment records in all. The self-hosted model got through the Aristotle set at roughly one claim a second. The collected biological works of Aristotle, assessed for empirical tractability, in about ten minutes. He took somewhat longer at the writing end.

Claims that survived triage went out as nanopublications: 880 of them signed and published on the first night, as standard RDF with trusty URIs, so each claim is a permanent, individually citable object rather than a line in our database. There are 8,890 nanopublication files in the repository, covering both the claims themselves and the machine assessments of them.

After that a claim has three honest fates. It can be proved — 91 of them are theorems with a proof, 73 of those checked by the Lean kernel, including Kimura's neutral substitution rate, Fisher's fundamental theorem and Maynard Smith's twofold cost of sex. It can be tested against data. Or it can be parked with the reason it cannot be tested written down, which is less satisfying and much more common.

The testing is where it gets uncomfortable in a useful way. Every test is pre-registered: the hypothesis and the pass/fail criteria are committed before anything is downloaded, with a SHA-256 on every file that comes in, so we cannot quietly discover that we meant the other threshold all along. Sixteen claims went the whole distance in the design repository — 6 supported, 5 refuted, 3 mixed, 2 honestly inconclusive for want of data. Thompson's scaling claim came back supported with a measured exponent of 2.742. Maynard Smith on hitchhiking held up at Spearman rho 0.616. Kimura's heterozygosity prediction was refuted, at an OLS slope of 0.107. So was one of Darwin's.

Across the project as a whole, 174 claims were tested against data: 93 supports, 37 mixed, 30 refutes, 14 inconclusive. Roughly a third of the verdicts go against the author being tested, which is the number we are proudest of, because a pipeline that only ever agrees with Darwin is not a pipeline, it is a fan club. All of it is pinned: one attestation file carries the SHA-256 of 1,117 artifacts at a single commit, timestamped by GitHub receipt at 14:49:40 UTC on October 31st, so the pre-registrations can be shown to predate the results rather than merely claiming to.

leanbio.title: The laws the fish had to obey
leanbio.standfirst: We wrote classical population genetics into a proof assistant, tried to break the proofs sixty-three times, and then made the flying fish answer to them.
body: Somewhere in the middle of MorphoLemma there is a library of biology written in a language that will not let you lie. Lean 4 is a proof assistant: you state a claim, you supply the argument, and a small program called the kernel checks every step before it agrees. Nothing is taken on authority, including yours. What we built in it is a real library rather than a sketch — 192 theorems and 60 lemmas across 16 core modules, 3,803 lines in those modules and 5,933 lines across the full source tree of 51 files, compiled against a pinned Mathlib revision on Lean 4.35.0, with not a single `sorry` anywhere in it. (`sorry` is Lean's word for a hole you promise to fill later. The count is zero, which is the only interesting number it can have.)

Four named classical results of mathematical biology are in there, proved from first principles rather than cited. Kimura's neutral substitution rate: harmless mutations accumulate in a lineage at a pace set by the mutation rate and nothing else, which is why a gene can tick like a clock. Kimura's neutral fixation probability, the odds that one new harmless variant eventually takes over the whole population, with an explicit error bound and a worked Wright-Fisher instance so it attaches to an actual model of breeding. Fisher's fundamental theorem, which ties how fast a population improves to how much fitness variation it has lying around. And Maynard Smith's twofold cost of sex, the uncomfortable observation that an otherwise identical asexual lineage reproduces twice as fast. There is also a new lower bound on fixation, proved outright — a favored or neutral lineage sitting at i of M gene copies fixes with probability at least i/M — and Haldane's cost of selection, derived from a hypothesis we left deliberately unproved and *named* as such, the one law of the 41 in the ledger that rests on a named premise rather than on nothing at all.

A proof assistant can still be gamed by quietly assuming what you wanted. So a dedicated audit module prints the axiom dependencies of each theorem, and for 182 of them the list stops at Lean's three standard axioms — propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound — and goes no further. Then we tried to break the library on purpose: 63 deliberately corrupted versions of 57 of the theorems were compiled, and Lean rejected all 63 — 62 of them at elaboration, on unsolved goals, type mismatches, failed tactics and `decide` cheerfully proving the negation, and one in the kernel itself. Nineteen control mutants, broken in ways that should still compile, all still compiled. The proofs have been attacked, not merely run once on a good day.

The laws do not sit in a file admiring themselves. A constraint set generated from the theorems — 51 of them now, each naming its lemma and its module — descends onto seven candidate ledgers of claims about the designed organism, 32 to 51 constraints per ledger depending on when each was run. Thirty-one candidates have been eliminated across those seven ledgers, each elimination carrying a Lean certificate that compiles — 32 certificates in all, the genotype ledger having proved one of its eliminations twice. The registry holds 62 law files, released through versions up to lawset 1.8.1, four of them **discovered from the project's own flying-fish measurements** rather than read out of a book, and `constraints.lean: must-hold` is injected into every parsed design whether the user asks for it or not.

Then we pointed the whole library at the animal. A 152-theorem audit instantiated every statement on real Exocoetidae data: 35 hold, 14 have their hypotheses violated, and 103 are marked cannot-evaluate with the missing measurement named row by row. The 14 are the good part. They fail because Davenport's 1992 measurements show flying fish do not grow as scale models of themselves — fin area scales as 1.834 where simple geometry wants 2, wing loading as 1.236 where it wants 1. The theorems were right. The fish simply declined to be a cube.

mcp.title: Everything, Callable
mcp.standfirst: We exposed the whole organism-design system as 64 named tools an agent can call, deployed it, and then pre-registered an experiment to find out whether a swarm of agents uses it better than one.
body: Somewhere between "we built a thing" and "anyone can use the thing" there is a layer of plumbing that nobody writes blog posts about. We wrote the plumbing, so here is the post. Every part of MorphoLemma — the parser that reads a sentence, the anatomy builder, the gene lookups, the growth curves, the aerodynamics — is exposed as a named tool that a software agent can call. One contract file declares 58 of them with full input and output schemas across 2,723 lines. A second server registers 39 live tools for the claims and proof side of the project. Between the two there are 64 distinct tool names, which is to say: 64 separate things you can ask the system to do without reading a line of its source.

It is not a local-only demo. The claims and proof server is deployed and answering on the public internet: send a tools/list request to the hosted endpoint and it returns 31 tools; ask its health endpoint and it reports its version and the 4,295 files it is serving. The hosted build withholds exactly one tool — `lean_propose`, the one that would run a Lean build on source you send it — which leaves 38 hosted against 39 over local stdio, and it forces every network and BLAST flag off regardless of what the caller asks for. The nine tools that write files never reach the server at all; they live only on the 58-tool sim-engine command line. The instance currently deployed is two minor versions behind the repository (0.6.1 against 0.8.1) and still serves five forum write tools, so the public surface is narrowed by construction, not yet sealed. There is also a command-line version that calls every registered tool by exactly the same name, plus a packaging test that unpacks the published archive and runs the whole pipeline from it, so "it works on my machine" is a claim the test suite can refute.

The part we are quietly proudest of is the shape of the answers. Fifty-three of the 58 handlers return the same envelope: the result, where each number came from, what the answer covers, the counts behind it, and a field called *weakest_input* that names the shakiest thing the answer rests on. The remaining five, all `leanbio_*`, return the shorter form — result, provenance, scope. Provenance is tagged with six levels that distinguish a measurement from a measurement someone else made from a number borrowed from a different species from a number we simply chose. The contract states in writing that a calibrated quantity may never be cited as a result. Most systems are built to produce a confident number. This one is built to tell you which number to distrust.

Taken to its logical end, this produces a tool that refuses to endorse itself. Call `validate_generation` on a designed organism and it runs five independently gated assessments across ten biological scales, seven of which it can actually assess. In the recorded run, two gates failed, two could not be assessed, and the tool declined to use the word "validated" — while handing back an itemised list of why, and a composite score of 0.4676 clearly labelled as not the verdict. One of those failing gates was the aerodynamics: 0.67 metres per second of reachable launch speed against the 8.64 needed for flight. The simulator computed that cleanly, which is the point. Underneath it all, 388 numeric constants in the simulation code were each chased to a source — 258 confirmed, 6 found wrong and corrected, 3 admitted unsourceable. Before that audit, 122 of them had no source at all.

And because an agent surface invites the obvious question of whether many agents beat one, we pre-registered an answer. The protocol fixed the model, the two allowed tools, the prompt, the output schema, the 12-turn cap and the budget identically across four arms on the same frozen set of 20 claims, before anything ran. Scoring was done by a mechanical checker with no language model in it: extract every DOI and URL, resolve each one over HTTP, count what survives. A single agent verified 12 of 20; isolated workers 16; a centralised swarm 18; a decentralised one 17. Zero fabricated identifiers in any arm. The whole experiment cost $16.98 and 10.5 minutes of wall clock, consuming 9.80 million tokens, and the accompanying deviations file logs every departure from the plan with timestamps — including the disclosure that the comparison was not blind to the held-out group, which cuts against our own result. Writing that down was the cheapest part of the build and probably the most useful.

studio.title: A Sentence Becomes an Organism
studio.standfirst: How one typed sentence becomes a nine-layer organism: five anatomical layers of real ontology terms, 359,703 gene links, 110 named meshes and, at the bottom, a single amino acid.
body: You type a sentence. Something like "a flying-fish with enlarged pectoral fins that glides above the water." What comes back is not a picture of a fish. It is an organism specified down to individual cells, individual genes, and in one place an individual amino acid.

The first step is a parser, and it is deliberately stupid in the way good tools are stupid: rule-based, no language model, no network call. The same sentence always produces the same specification — run it twice and the bytes are identical — which means you can argue with it. Given "a zebrafish with large wing-like pectoral fins that can glide," it returns a spec that validates clean and carries exactly one hard criterion — glide, feasible, at the adult stage — no editable parameters, four assumptions it had to make, and the fin clause itself handed straight back under *unparsed*: "a with large wing-like pectoral fins that". Words outside its closed vocabulary get no spec at all, just a failed validation with the errors named. A tool that tells you which of your words it ignored is doing something most software has decided is impolite.

Then the descent. The design drops through five anatomical layers of real, existing ontology terms: body, then organ system, then organ, then tissue, then cell. For the flying fish it resolves the animal to NCBITaxon_76072 — the family Exocoetidae — and returns one body, 13 organ systems, 67 distinct organs, 198 tissues and 257 cell types, assembled from 12 queries to Ubergraph, a public ontology database. Every node is a real identifier someone else maintains; every edge carries the query that produced it; and in the blueprint tool every SPARQL response is cached under the SHA-256 of the query text, all 157 cache files committed, so a fresh copy of the project rebuilds those five layers from the 12 cached queries with the network unplugged — and `--offline` fails loudly rather than quietly reaching out.

Those nodes are hooks, and things hang off them. A vetted gene map holds 359,703 links from genes to body structures across 52,517 proxy-fish genes — 30,010 zebrafish, 22,499 medaka and 8 that are not species-specific — each typed as *expressed in* (349,658 of them), *required for* (10,042), or *sufficient for* (three). Every one of those links is a zebrafish or medaka record; nobody has measured a flying fish this way. The pectoral fin alone has 982 genes expressed in it and 166 required for it. Genes sufficient to enlarge it: exactly one, called kcnk5b. Underneath sits an index of 913,921 molecular annotation rows across five layers of biology, covering 3,860 genes against 1,416 anatomical parts.

Below that, the organism acquires a body, a childhood and a bloodstream. One reproducible Blender script emits 110 individually named meshes — 40 vertebrae with their spines, 14 fin rays per side, a cleithrum, a scapula — each tagged with its ontology identifier and split left from right so the fish can be opened like a book. A developmental model built from 318 logged data requests puts it on a growth curve from egg to adult. A 28-node circulation graph carries oxygen from water through gills, blood, heart and muscle to mechanical power. And at the bottom, a 35-species sequence ladder reaches the residues themselves, where position 326 of one transporter gene reads L in both gliding halfbeaks and eight of nine flying fishes, and F in all 24 non-gliders, with an I in the saury.

All of this is one command-line tool with 58 callable functions, and 53 of them return the same envelope: the result, where it came from, what it covers, the counts, and — the field I would put in everything — the weakest input the answer rests on. Sixty-two formal mathematical laws are injected into every design as must-hold, whether or not you asked for them. The parser mentions this in its assumptions, politely, the way a contractor mentions the building code.

harness.title: The Part That Says No
harness.standfirst: Nine real alignments, a wind-tunnel-calibrated flight simulator, and a 57,774-item sealed benchmark: the machinery built to tell us whether our fish could fly.
body: A design is only as good as the thing willing to reject it, so most of the effort went into the part that does the rejecting. It starts with real sequences. Nine genes were aligned with MAFFT v7.526 in its most careful mode (L-INS-i, `--localpair --maxiterate 1000`): 364 sequence rows across 6,819 alignment columns and 54 distinct animals — zebrafish, medaka, three bats, mouse, human, two colugos, a sugar glider, two geckos, a snake, and 35 beloniform species. Those rows come from five places, and Ensembl release 116 is the minority partner: 210 are Daane et al. 2021's captured exons projected onto medaka residues, 80 are longest-isoform RefSeq proteins from NCBI, 65 are Ensembl REST 116 orthologue proteins, 7 come from the published *Hirundichthys speculiger* proteome on figshare, and 2 are local tblastn projections. Ensembl 116's zebrafish proteome is also the reference the orthology calls and the variant residues were checked against. A beloniform row is dropped when its captured exons cover less than 30% of the medaka protein, and every alignment file names the species it dropped and why. Low-coverage columns, by contrast, are never dropped: they are painted in a fourth colour meaning NO DATA — identical, substitution, indel, no data, four entries in the legend on the validation page — so a gap can never be misread as agreement. It is not a rare case: 399 of prdm1a's 1,410 columns are no-data, and 201 of kcnh2a's 1,451, while tbx5a is covered end to end. Against the real flying fishes, zebrafish identity runs from 56.3% at *kcnk5b* to 82.4% at *tbx5a*.

That panel exists to answer one question honestly: how big is the edit we are proposing? The answer is computed rather than asserted. Our winged zebrafish differs from its reference by **2 edited loci and 1 amino acid**. Zebrafish and medaka, two ordinary laboratory fishes, differ by about **7,300 amino-acid substitutions** across just the 37 proteins in the causal chain that have medaka counterparts. Against a bat it is 10,205. Nature does not design organisms by touching two genes, and the harness says so in a number.

Then the physics. The simulator works from first principles with sourced constants: weight, the minimum speed at which a given wing can hold a given body up, the gliding bound that the Lean layer proves, a two-phase glide range, the power level flight demands, and a ceiling set by how much oxygen the animal can actually move. Its lift and drag figures — a maximum lift coefficient of 0.78 and a best glide ratio of 4.37 — are not guesses; they come from Park and Choi's 2010 wind-tunnel measurements of a stuffed flying fish, a sentence I have enjoyed writing more than is probably appropriate. A measured 14% drag reduction from flying close to the water is included. Every criterion is carried through a 400-draw ensemble of the uncertain inputs.

It passes its controls, 5 of 5, and 121 of 121 physics tests. A real adult flying fish launched at 15 m/s is predicted to glide 36.5 metres against a 10-metre threshold, which sits reasonably beside the roughly 50 metres the field literature reports — though we flag that agreement as partly circular, since the launch speed and the field distance come from the same body of observations. The control that matters more is the one where we removed the wings in software: the same animal, the same launch speed, and now 15.00 m/s reachable against 21.75 m/s required. The gate is reading wing area, not species labels. Which is exactly why its verdict on our own design is worth believing: 0.67 m/s reachable against 8.64 m/s needed. The two edits did move the required speed from the unmodified zebrafish's 13.03 m/s down to 8.64, a real 34% reduction in the right direction, and the harness notes without flinching that 0 of 400 draws get off the water. A validator that cannot fail the thing its authors wanted is not a validator.

Underneath all of it sits a frozen benchmark of **57,774 labelled organism-plausibility items** — 34,419 for development, 23,355 sealed away — covering 13,606 real fish species across 560 families, with the pre-registration hashed before anything was scored and the held-out half kept from the scorer's own author. Four scorer versions ran, each pre-registered, none overwritten: area under the curve went 0.937 then 0.994, 98.7% of held-out real species were called plausible, and across five different random splits the score varied by 0.0001.

One result from that benchmark travels beyond this project. A synthetic organism built by shuffling real traits cannot be caught by per-trait ranges at all, however carefully tuned: 25 envelopes over 20 traits scored 0.498, a coin flip, because the fakes keep every individual measurement where real fish live and break only the relationships between them. Adding a single joint term — the design's own family exactly subtracted out first — took it to 0.823. In the same spirit, the 73-requirement functional ledger leads with coverage, 22 of 73 assessable, rather than the flattering fraction of those that passed, and that number is kept out of the composite score entirely. Labels like that are what make the rest of the numbers quotable.
